summary: YvyShift is a free web app that helps farmers and agronomists choose a winter crop rotation that holds up in dry years. It compares four real Paraguayan rotations (fallow, wheat, black oat cover crop and second-crop maize after soybean) against 25 seasons of daily NASA POWER data, using an FAO-56 water balance that runs entirely in the browser. Farmers set their own priorities, and every score separates what NASA data measure (water deficit, heat and frost) from what the farmer values (soil cover, extra harvests and crop diversity). Without any tuning, the model’s water deficit tracks real FAO soybean yield losses over 23 seasons (r = −0.83) and agrees with MODIS greenness and ERA5 rainfall. It matters because the 2021–22 drought halved Paraguay’s soybean harvest, and most farmers have no simple way to test a rotation against past droughts before they plant. YvyShift works offline after the first visit, needs no account, speaks six languages including Guaraní, and runs for any point on Earth.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
YvyShift is a free web app that helps farmers and extension agronomists choose a winter crop rotation that holds up in dry years. It was built for eastern Paraguay, where soybean dominates and the 2021–22 drought halved the national harvest, and it works for any point on Earth.
The user picks a location: one of eight soybean areas of eastern Paraguay stored in the app (Itapúa, Alto Paraná, Canindeyú, San Pedro, Caaguazú, Caazapá, Amambay and Misiones), any point in the world downloaded live from the NASA POWER API, or a field drawn on the map or imported as GeoJSON. Then the user chooses a climate scenario: a typical year (the median of 25 seasons), a bad year (the 80th percentile of each risk, about 1 in 5), El Niño or La Niña seasons (NOAA Oceanic Niño Index), or one real past season such as 2021–22. The user sets a soil class (sand, loam or clay, FAO-56 Table 19) or the pure climate baseline, removes crops they do not grow, and sets priorities from 0 to 5 for six criteria: water deficit, heat at flowering, frost at the sensitive stage, soil cover, commercial harvests per year and crop diversity.
A JavaScript engine runs an FAO-56 water balance in 10-day steps over 25 seasons (2001–02 to 2025–26). Reference evapotranspiration uses the Hargreaves-Samani equation with NASA POWER temperature and top-of-atmosphere radiation (TOA_SW_DWN); crop demand is ETc = Kc × ET0, and a soil bucket tracks the water stored in the root zone. It compares four real Paraguayan rotations: A, soybean then winter fallow; B, soybean then wheat; C, soybean then black oat cover crop; D, early soybean then second-crop maize. Users can also build their own rotation.

What benefits does it have?
Field DNA turns 25 seasons into one picture of dry, hot and frosty years, so a farmer can see how often a 2021–22 could happen again before choosing what to plant. Every score is split into what NASA data measure (water, heat, frost) and what the farmer values (soil cover, harvests, diversity), so the trade-off is visible: a cover crop protects the soil but costs water. The Resilience Passport is a printable report with the evidence and its sources, for a cooperative, a bank or an agronomist. The app needs no account or API key, works offline after the first visit, has a high-contrast Sun mode for outdoor use, and speaks six languages (Spanish, English, Guaraní, Portuguese, Japanese and Hindi; the Guaraní still needs review by a native speaker).

What is the intended impact?
The 2022 National Agricultural Census counted 3,009,608 ha of soybean in eastern Paraguay, producers expected about 3.6 million ha in 2025/26, and about 39,000 smallholders (under 20 ha) planted around 20 % of the soybean area in 2017. YvyShift gives them and their technicians a free way to test a rotation against 25 real seasons before planting. Because it runs on NASA POWER, it works anywhere: a one-click demo runs the same model for Iowa, USA.

What tools did you use?
HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with no backend; everything is computed in the browser. Node.js runs 34 automated tests. Git and GitHub, Playwright for interface checks, and Claude (Anthropic) as a development assistant for code, text and translations, as stated in the app footer and the code headers. Data: NASA POWER (LaRC), MODIS MOD13Q1 and HLS through NASA GIBS and the ORNL DAAC, NOAA ONI, FAOSTAT and ERA5 for validation. An optional local AI assistant (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, about 0.9 GB, through WebLLM on WebGPU) runs on the user’s device, asks before downloading, is restricted to farming topics, and removes any number that does not come from the app’s own results; it labels its answers and can still be wrong. No special hardware is needed; the AI needs a device with WebGPU.

How is it creative?
It is built around the decision a Paraguayan farmer really makes every winter (fallow, wheat, black oat or second-crop maize), not a generic crop map. The “Show NASA data only” button keeps only the climate part of the score, and it openly shows that fallow wins on climate alone: extra crops cost water. Instead of hiding that result, the app makes it the core message: NASA data show what each extra crop costs in water, and the farmer decides what that water is worth. The home page shows the same Itapúa fields from space in the 2022 drought and in 2024, and the assistant understands common Guaraní farm words.

What factors did the team consider?
Validation with no tuning: the model’s water deficit tracks FAO soybean yield losses over 23 seasons (r = −0.83); four of the five worst real harvests are among the model’s five driest seasons (chance ≈ 0.27 %); NASA POWER rain agrees with ERA5 over 24 seasons (r = 0.74 and 0.85), and the deficit agrees with MODIS January greenness over 25 seasons (r = −0.76 in Itapúa). Every figure can be recomputed with one command from the repository. Scale: a NASA POWER cell is about 56 × 62 km in Itapúa, so the climate is regional even when the field images are 30 m. Honest limits: soil classes are generic, pests and prices are not modelled, and second-crop maize in rotation D is evaluated only up to 30 April, so its late frost risk may be underestimated. The tool compares and explores; it does not predict yields or tell the farmer what to plant.
